prompt.context: Our client is a national Aerospace company that focuses on creating space programs. For the past few years, there has not been a reusable platform for software to be shared across programs. The client is doing well, but wonders if they should develop an interface to have software shared among programs. It makes sense, but the client suspects it might be too expensive.
prompt.question: The client wants you to help decide whether to develop this shared software interface, and if so, how to go about it.

clarifying_info.q: Why is the client considering this initiative now?
clarifying_info.a: SpaceZ has been losing a lot of bids recently to its competitors due to its higher priced quotes. The government is becoming cost conscious and bids can no longer be revised (used to be able to get more money from the government if underbid).
The customer is the government; SpaceZ operates only in the US market.

clarifying_info.q: Do the programs currently communicate with each other?
clarifying_info.a: Programs do not talk to each other — no communication between projects and no sharing of lessons learned. Over 90% of projects are classified and shared on a need-to-know basis only.

clarifying_info.q: Are there near-term opportunities where this platform could be used?
clarifying_info.a: The client has eight near-term proposals to be submitted within a year for new projects/contracts; they want to use this platform to be more competitive.

clarifying_info.q: What are the options for building this platform?
clarifying_info.a: Three options exist: greenfield (build from scratch), partnerships (two sub-options: enterprise/Option 1 or individual/Option 2), and acquisition.

exhibits.title: Annual Cost of the Three Options — Table
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of four options (Acquisition, Partnership Enterprise, Partnership Individual, Greenfield) across five cost dimensions: Set Up Fee, Labor, Time Frame to Completion, Increase in Maintenance Cost, and Number of Users in Year 1.

exhibits.title: Annual Cost of the Three Options — Bar Chart
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing annual costs over six years (Year 1–6) for Acquisition, Partnership (Enterprise/Option 1), and Greenfield.

framework: Understand the strategic objective: cost reduction to win more government bids — NOT revenue generation
Identify all three pathways: Greenfield (build), Partnership (partner), Acquisition (buy)
Screen options against near-term constraint: must be usable within 1 year for 8 upcoming proposals
Quantify costs for surviving options: set-up fee + labor + ongoing maintenance
Compare total cost of each option over a multi-year horizon
Assess risks and flexibility of each remaining option

questions.prompt: Which option(s) can be eliminated immediately based on the near-term proposal timeline, and why?
questions.guidance: Both Acquisition (1.5 years to complete) and Greenfield (2 years to complete) exceed the 1-year window needed to use the platform in the eight near-term proposals. Candidate should eliminate both without doing heavy math, citing the timeline constraint.

questions.prompt: Calculate the first-year cost for Partnership Option 1 (Enterprise).
questions.guidance: Sum set-up fee + labor for 0.5 year + maintenance for 0.5 year.

math.setup: Set up fee + (Labor rate × 0.5 yr) + (Maintenance rate × 0.5 yr)

questions.prompt: Calculate the first-year cost for Partnership Option 2 (Individual) using an estimated 5 users.
questions.guidance: Same structure as Option 1 but maintenance is per-user. Use 5 users as the estimated minimum (adjustable). Note that costs will increase as user count grows year over year.

math.setup: Set up fee + (Labor rate × 0.5 yr) + (Maintenance per user × users × 0.5 yr)
math.answer: $115,000 in Year 1; $5,000+/year thereafter (rising as users grow)

questions.prompt: At what user count does Partnership Option 2 (Individual) become more expensive per year than Option 1 (Enterprise)?
questions.guidance: In steady state (after Year 1), Option 1 costs $100,000/year in maintenance. Option 2 costs $2,000 × N users/year. Set equal and solve for N.

math.answer: At 50 users per year, Option 2 becomes as expensive as Option 1; above 50 users Option 1 is cheaper.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the risks of going with Partnership Option 2 (Individual)?

categories.name: Vendor/Partner Risk
ideas: Chosen partner does not live up to its reputation for reliability
Partner could be acquired or exit the market
Partner may raise per-user pricing over time

categories.name: Scalability Risk
ideas: Per-user cost structure becomes expensive as team grows beyond 50 users
May need to renegotiate or switch to enterprise edition, incurring transition costs

categories.name: Security/Classification Risk
ideas: Over 90% of projects are classified; sharing a third-party platform raises need-to-know concerns
Data governance controls must be validated before rollout

categories.name: Integration Risk
ideas: Labor cost exists because integration and support services from the partner are required
Delays in integration could jeopardize near-term proposals

recommendation: Choose Partnership Option 2 (Individual) to minimize upfront investment given uncertainty, as this is the first time the company is undertaking this initiative
Keep Option 1 (Enterprise) in mind as a natural upgrade path once users exceed 50
Immediately apply the new platform to the eight near-term government proposals to submit more competitive bids
risks: The chosen partner may not deliver on quality or reliability promises
Per-user maintenance costs will rise as adoption scales, eventually exceeding Option 1 costs above 50 users
Classification and need-to-know requirements may limit platform adoption or require additional security controls
next_steps: Move to the enterprise edition once user count exceeds 50
Use the result of this project in the immediate eight proposals to put forth competitive bids
Establish clear SLAs and performance metrics with the chosen partner
Evaluate security and clearance requirements for classified programs before full rollout
